full_judgment:
Ranadhir Sen, J:- This Rule, at the instance of the plaintiff, is directed against the order dated 16.6.80 of the learned Subordinate judge, refusing the plaintiff’s prayer for attachment before judgment under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 2. Plaintiff filed Money Suit No. 23 of 1980 for recovery of certain sum of money and made the following prayer: 

 "for a decree against the defendant No. 1 for realisation of money amounting to Tk. 3,27,02,361/61 (Taka three chore twenty seven lac two thousand and three hundred sixty one and paisa sixty one) only payable by the defendant No. 1 to the plaintiff and also interest @ 12% on the said amount till realisation of the decretal amount" 

 The suit was filed on 19.5.80 On the same day an application for attachment before judgment under Order 38 rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed on behalf of the plaintiff in the said petition the plaintiff stated as follows:- 

 "1. That the plaintiff petitioner has instituted the above-mentioned money suit for realisation of unpaid price against the defendant No. 1, to the tune of Tk. 3,27,02,361/61. 

 2. That the plaintiff-petitioner has a very fair chance of success and obtaining decree for the said amount of Tk. 3,27,02,361/61 against the defendant No. 3, from this learned Court. 

 iii) Tk. 3,27,02,361/61 in China Barter Account lying with Sonali Bank, Local Officer, Foreign Exchange Department, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dacca, the defendant No. 2 out of the amount allocated in favour of the defendant No. 1, in the form of L/Cs. Nos. 79/297047 and 79/207057 and other L/Cs. in the name of the defendant No. 1 or its transferees including Export Performances Licences so that the decree when passed in the above suit may be satisfied. 5. That unless the properties of the defendant No. 1 as have been detailed in para 4 above are attached before judgment the decree obtained in the suit by the plaintiff shall be frustrated and on execution of the decree in the above mentioned suit nothing would be available for the plaintiff to satisfy the decree that may be obtained by the plaintiff. Wherefore, it is most humbly prayed that your honour would be pleased to direct the defendant to furnish security for the properties described in paragraph 4 or to direct the defendant No. 1 to appear at the Court and show cause why he should not furnish security to the extent of the claimed amount of Tk. 2, 27, 02,361/61 and in the meantime pass an order of conditional attachment of the said properties for the ends of justice." 

 In the meantime the property mentioned in sub-parts (ii) and (iii) of para 4 in the petition be provisionally attached subject to furnishing security Urgent requisites at once." Defendant No. 1, in obedience to the aforesaid notice, appeared and filed objection against the plaintiff's prayer for attachment before judgment, denying the material allegations of the plaintiff. Defendant No: 1 contended that the properties in the concerned letters of credit belonged to the principal, viz, the Chaina buyer. It was further stated that the application for attachment before judgment was not maintainable inasmuch as vague and indefinite allegations have been made in the application. An affidavit-in-opposition was filed by the plaintiff against the affidavit filed on behalf of defendant No. 1. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the facts and materials on record available before him rejected the application for attachment before judgment and vacated the ad-interim order of attachment granted by him on 20.5.80 the learned Subordinate Judge was of the view that the petition for a attachment before judgment suffered from insufficient materials. He observed as follows: 

 "From these words it cannot be said that the defendant No. 1 is about to dispose of his property or remove it from the jurisdiction of the court with the object of obstructing or delaying the execution of the decree that may be passed against him in this suit when the defdt No. 1 was absolutely in dark about filing of this suit. In order to attach the property before judgment u/s 38 rule 5 C.P.C. there must be some material facts and specific allegations against the defdt No. 1 that he is going to dispose of whole or any part of his properties to frustrate the execution of decree that may be passed which are very much absent here in this petition. The allegations which the plaintiff has made in para 3 of the petition are vague and general allegations and as such it cannot be considered for exercising the powers conferred in Order 38, rule 5 C.P.C. and in this connection the decision reported in 27 D.L.R. page 256 and 31 D.L.R. page 112 (A.D) may be referred." 

 "The rule does not provide any scope to attach item No. 3 of the petition as the defdt No. 1 is not the absolute owner of this property. I do agree with the content ion of the .learned Advocate for the defdt No. 1. In view of the facts discussed above I am of the opinion that the plaintiff has failed to make out a case for getting an order of attachment before judgment." 

 4. This Rule was obtained by the plaintiff on 23 June, 1980. The Rule was made returnable. 

 This proposition initially provided for the basis and sanctity of 4 letter of credit in the international commercial world. With the advancement of international trade and commerce, the concept of promise appears to have assumed an improved character as we gather from Uniform Commercial Code, 1972 Official. Text with comments and appendix and the Uniform customs and practice for documentary credits. We refreshed our ideas as to how commercial letters of credits are dealt with in international trade and commerce from the treatise of A. G. Davis, "The law relating to Commercial Letters of Credit." We have also considered the relevant provisions of Negotiable Instruments Act in this connection. On consideration of these authorities it appears that the state of promise is indeed the starting point of international commercial transactions. Initially the property in a letter of credit belongs to the buyer who places his money in a bank of his country. It then becomes the property of the bank according to the terms of contract between the buyer and his bank. In the seller's country, the buyer's bank Issues a request with the promise in terms of the conditions contained in the contract between the parties. On the fulfillment of the terms as contained in the contract, the seller's bank performs its part in the international transactions. Benficiary under the letter of credit holds the property under certain terms So also the Bank in the seller's country. In this view of the matter, Mr. Asrarul Hossain the learned Advocate appearing for defendant No. 2 Sonali Bank has rightly contended that ownership of the property in the letters of credit rests with the persons variously under changing circumstances. The contention appears to be of substance. The authorities referred to above lend support in favour of the contention. In the facts of the instant case it appears that the ownership in the property of the letters of credit is disputed. Mr. Pal contends that it is not the property of defendant No. 1 whereas Mr. Faqir Shahabuddin Ahmed contends that it is the property of defendant No. 1. The bank appears to have taken a neutral position con-tending that it depends on the decision of the Court to whom the ownership of the property in the letters of credit belongs. The Subordinate Judge has found that "defendant No. 1 is not the absolute owner of this property." In such circumstances contention of Mr. Faqir Shahabuddin Ahmed that the properties in the letters of credit belongs to defendant No. 1 does not stand on a sound footing. In the exercise of revisional jurisdiction we are not called upon to determine a question of fact as to whether or not the property in the relevant letters of credit belongs either to the plaintiffs or defendant No.1 or the bank. Evidently the letters of credit other than No. 79/207047 and No. 79/207057 have no nexus in the dispute between the parties. Those other letters of credits are not liable to be attached in any view of the matter. It is not for us to say anything with regard to the performance of the parties. We have been addressed by the learned Advocates that there were defaults on the part of the plaintiff and that there were ladles and non-compliance of the part of defendant No. 1. We do not intend to express our opinion in this behalf. In the exercise of revisional jurisdiction we are not called upon to express our opinion as to the beneficiary's rights under the two letters of credit mentioned earlier. The contention of Mr. Pal that a letter of credit is a mere promise does not appear to stand on a sound footing. In our opinion it is a property. We have already indicated that ownership in the property of the relevant letters of credit is in dispute. Now, the question arises whether such a disputed property is attachable. It has been argued on behalf of the plaintiff that section 60 is no bar to attachment of the property in the letter of credit in question. Section 60 may not be bar, but unless a prima facie ownership of the property is determined, the same is not liable to be attached by an order of the Court. The plaintiff in this behalf appears to have signally failed to make out a prima facie case. We have already quoted the petition for attachment before judgment. Paragraph 3 of the petition appears to be significantly vague. In that paragraph only an apprehension has been expressed without indicating the corresponding objectivity behind the apprehension. The learned Subordinate Judge, in our opinion, correctly construed the application for attachment before judgment and rightly refused the prayer for attachment before judgment. In this behalf, we may also refer to the case of Md. Shamsul Huda v. Mozammel Huq W. In this decision we may profitably quote the following observations of their Lordships:— 

 "The power which has been conferred on the Court under the said provision is an extraordinary power whereby a party in the suit may be prevented from use and enjoyment of its own properties, before any decree has at all been passed against him, and when there is no certainty that a decree will at all be passed against him. This power must, therefore, be used with utmost caution and should be sparingly exercised. It is clear that before issuing an order under the said provisions of the Code, the Court must be satisfied that the defendant has been trying to frustrate the effect of the decree that may be passed against him by disposing of his property or re-moving it from the jurisdiction of the court. That is to say, the Court must be satisfied not only that the defendant is about to dispose of his property or remove it from its jurisdiction but also that this disposal or removal is with the object of obstructing or delaying the execution of any decree that may be passed against him. This satisfaction, however, is to be judicial satisfaction and it must be based on some materials which are to be found in the affidavit filed by the party or otherwise. It is true that an order of attachment under this provision is to be found in the affidavit filed by the party or otherwise. It is true that an order of attachment under this provision is to be passed on the basis of an application made by the plaintiff and an order of conditional attachment may be passed even experte. It is, of course, to be borne in mind that it is difficult to produce any conclusive evidence before the Court to prove the intention of a party which is secretly conceived and sought to be suppeptiously executed, but even then, there must be some concrete allegations before the Court about the actions of the defendant and some materials in support thereof. Otherwise, this provision of law is likely to be turned into an instrument of oppression and great harassment." 

 (2) The plaintiff shall, unless the Court other-wise directs, specify the property required to be attached and the estimated value thereof, 

 13. On a consideration of the questions raised in this Rule we are of the view that the plaintiff has failed to make out a case for attachment before judgment under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The allegations made in the paragraph 3 of the petition are vague, general, without materials in proof and insufficient to warrant the jurisdiction of the Court under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that view of the matter, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. 

 17. On a perusal of the application for addition of parties we are not inclined to allow the prayer at this stage. The plaintiff, if necessary, may file an appropriate application before the trial Court for addition of the proposed parties. The application is accordingly rejected.
